newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bajaj Auto 97/98 net lowered.
newsitem.headline: India's Bajaj Auto 97/98 net lowered.

text.p: Indian scooter and motorcycle maker Bajaj Auto's vehicle sales are likely to remain sluggish during the first six months of the current 1997/98 financial year, analysts said on Thursday.

Analysts polled by Reuters said they had lowered their net profit forecasts for the year ending March 31, 1998 by 7-12 percent to 5.0 billion-5.3 billion rupees after the firm released its 1996/97 results on Wednesday.
Bajaj Auto -- among the world's largest makers of two- and three-wheelers -- announced a modest five percent rise in net profit to 4.40 billion rupees, from 4.18 billion in 1995/96.
Chairman Rahul Bajaj said weak sales growth was due to an industrial slowdown that has seen depressed demand for consumer durables since the middle of calendar 1996.
"The first half of this year is also likely to be lacklustre. The recovery will probably set in during the second half," said K.N. Sreenivasan, automobile analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking.
He said an impending petroleum product hike and a low bonus ratio would weaken sentiment in the stock.

Bajaj's board is due to meet on May 19 to finalise an issue of bonus equity shares. The firm's chairman has said he is not in favour of issuing a bonus in the proportion of one share for every share held.
"Scooter and moped sales will also continue to be weak for the next couple of months," Sreenivasan said, adding that he was asking investors to buy the stock at declines.
"It makes sense to get in the stock at 750-800 rupees."
Most analysts said they were recommending investors "buy on weakness" but some pegged the entry level at around 830 rupees.
Bajaj Auto shares closed 28.25 rupees lower at 887 on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Thursday.
The firm said vehicle sales rose to 1.42 million units in 1996/97, from 1.31 million in the previous year.
Most analysts said they were targeting vehicle sales of 1.55 million vehicles in the current year.
Analysts said the cash-rich firm was likely to receive lower returns on investments due to falling interest rates.
"Other income will be much lower. If interest rates are going to fall, Bajaj will earn less as yields on their investments go down," said Rakesh Parekh, analyst at Caspian Securities.
Analysts said the sharply higher taxation at 2.36 billion rupees, against 1.77 billion in 1995/96 was also responsible for the profit downgrade in the current year.

Bajaj said leasing proposals worth 1.8 billion rupees had yielded a tax break for the firm in the previous year. But due to regulatory changes in 1996/97, the firm did not participate in such transactions, he said.
"We have removed lease income from the 1997/98 forecast," said Anupam Thareja, automobile analyst at HSBC B&K Securities.
He said a lease income of some 2.0 billion rupees would have added 300 million rupees to the firm's after tax profit in 1997/98.

"We're not looking at very much happening in the company, but no matter what analysts think, if the market starts looking good, investors make a beeline for Bajaj," said an analyst at a U.S. investment bank.
"There are benefits of being such a visible company."
